source.title: Optimal ridge penalty for real-world high-dimensional data can be zero or negative due to the implicit ridge regularization
source.authors: D. Kobak; Jonathan Lomond; Benoit Sanchez

page_placements.theme: Zero or negative optimal explicit ridge

record.file_problem: Full paper text is present; some mathematical symbols and formulas show OCR/encoding corruption.
record.tranche_reason: Tests whether risk falls again after interpolation as model dimensionality grows, but uses linear ridge-regression models rather than the original deep-network settings.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports risk as a function of ridge penalty and optimal penalties by dimensionality. Those results do not measure the size-, epoch-, or sample-wise curves named by most claim versions; cited results from other work are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The study's simulations sweep linear-model dimensionality (p, or p+q added random predictors) past n = 64. They report the minimum-norm risk rising toward p ≈ n and then falling again. They also report that the optimal-ridge risk shows no divergence at p = n. This bears on V4 in a non-deep model class and on V6's claim that optimal regularization removes the peak.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors also note that the gain of optimal ridge over minimum-norm OLS vanishes as p ≫ n, and that the optimal λ turns negative when β aligns with high-variance directions.
record.recipe_differences: Uses ridge regression and minimum-norm OLS in real high-dimensional datasets and spiked-covariance/random-feature simulations, rather than deep-network size sweeps or epoch-wise measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Risk and the optimal ridge penalty vary with predictor dimensionality, covariance structure, and the variance/count of added random predictors. In the spiked-covariance simulation, λopt becomes negative for sufficiently large p; the stated crossover is p ≳ 600 for the reported parameters.

fits_no_version.finding: In the overparameterized regime (p ≳ 600 in simulation; real genomics data; MNIST random Fourier features), positive ridge gives no gain over minimum-norm OLS, and the optimal λ is negative (−150 at p = 1000; ≈ −80 on MNIST).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Far past interpolation, implicit regularization from low-variance directions can make the optimal explicit ridge penalty zero or negative.

fits_no_version.finding: Augmenting with q random predictors of variance λ/q and using the minimum-norm estimator is proven asymptotically equivalent to ridge with penalty λ.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Overparameterization with low-variance features acts as implicit ridge regularization.

record.problems: The core dimensionality results are simulations under specified covariance and signal settings; the authors explicitly say the work does not explain highly nonlinear underdetermined models. Uncertainty intervals or error bars are not stated for the reported average risks.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the risk-versus-λ panels in Figures 1, 2a–d, and 6, or optimal-λ panels in Figures 2f, 3, and 4e: these measure penalty choice/risk at fixed settings, not the model-size, epoch, or sample-size curves in the tested versions. Figure 4b also plots the untruncated estimator, which the text says converges slightly more slowly to the same limit; omitted as secondary to the truncated-estimator result in r3.

untested.parts: Deep networks are not studied; the authors say the results do not explain deep nets.
No sample-wise risk curves; sample size is varied only for λopt (Fig. 3).
Initial falling arm of the U-curve (sweeps start near-optimal); model classes other than linear regression with Gaussian features.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Dependence of the peak on label noise (σ² fixed at 1); multiple or triple descent across model size.

record.verdict_notes: Subject kind should be linear regression, not toy network. The reader's V4 limits_scope label is dropped: the missing first arm reflects the chosen starting p, not a failure of the effect, so it is listed as untested. The reader validation issue is resolved by linking V6 to r2 only. Neither original source is this study.

versions.untested_parts: Deep-network test error across model sizes and its peak near the interpolation threshold.
Test error as training sample size increases near the interpolation threshold.

The linear-model experiments test dimensionality-dependent risk, but do not establish the generality of the curve across model classes; the pre-interpolation risk does not show the full classical U-shaped descent.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across axes.

The paper tests the effect of optimized ridge regularization on the risk near interpolation in one simulated setting. It does not test whether label noise drives the peak or whether multiple peaks occur.
No alternative effective parameter count is used to assess whether the second descent becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model
rows.operation_detail: Varied predictor dimensionality and measured expected normalized MSE for OLS/minimum-norm OLS.
rows.value: At p = 10, OLS yielded near-optimal performance; as p increased, each additional predictor increased OLS MSE. Near p ≈ n = 64, expected MSE became very large; at larger p, minimum-norm OLS MSE quickly decreased again.
rows.note: The reported curve has the rise toward interpolation and a second descent, but the text does not report an initial falling arm.
rows.check: Risk rises from p = 10 to a very large peak near p ≈ n = 64, then 'quickly decreased again' (Fig. 2e). The second descent appears in full. There is no initial falling arm, because p = 10 is already near-optimal in this design, so the classical U-arm is not shown rather than contradicted. Subject is a linear OLS/minimum-norm estimator, not a toy network.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V4. Risk rises toward p ≈ n = 64 and decreases again beyond interpolation. V4's post-interpolation improvement is directly observed.
source_check.problem: The partial state treats an unmeasured initial falling arm as incomplete evidence for V4, whose stated effect is post-interpolation improvement.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model, optimal ridge estimator
rows.operation_detail: Compared expected risk of the optimal ridge estimator across predictor dimensionalities with OLS/minimum-norm OLS and oracle risk.
rows.baseline: Minimum-norm OLS/OLS risk and oracle risk
rows.value: Optimal ridge risk was close to oracle risk across dimensionalities and did not show divergence at p = n.
rows.note: This reports the risk curve under optimized ridge regularization; the authors do not describe an initial fall in risk with dimensionality.
rows.check: This row bears on V6, not V4: it measures the optimally regularized risk, which was close to oracle and 'did not show any divergence at p = n'. Remove the V4 link. The baseline is the r1 unregularized curve.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model augmented with random predictors
rows.size_stated: p = 50 original predictors; q up to 400 additional predictors
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number q of random predictors, with each predictor variance set to λopt/q; measured risk of the truncated minimum-norm estimator.
rows.measure: Expected MSE versus number of random predictors q
rows.value: As p + q approached n, MSE increased; after p + q exceeded n, it decreased. q ≈ 200 was already close to the limiting performance.
rows.note: The reported curve shows a post-interpolation decrease, but not an initial falling arm.
rows.check: The MSE of the truncated estimator rises as p+q approaches n, then decreases and approaches the ridge limit by q ≈ 200 (Fig. 4b). The second descent is observed; there is no initial falling arm because the sweep starts at p = 50.

source_check.correct: State: observed for V4. With p = 50 and n = 64, MSE increases as p + q approaches n, decreases beyond n, and approaches the optimal-ridge limit by q ≈ 200.
source_check.problem: The post-interpolation improvement specified by V4 is observed; absence of an initial falling arm does not justify partial.

rows.subject: spiked covariance model augmented with random predictors
rows.size_stated: p = 50 original predictors; q up to 400 additional predictors
rows.operation_detail: Increased the number q of random predictors, each with variance 1; measured risk of the truncated minimum-norm estimator.
rows.measure: Expected MSE versus number of random predictors q
rows.value: The MSE curve had a minimum at a particular qopt; the text says that when q is above qopt, implicit regularization is too strong and additional positive ridge penalty cannot improve expected risk.
rows.note: The text reports a minimum and the regularization interpretation, but does not explicitly describe the full curve as a fall-rise-fall curve.
rows.check: The text reports only a minimum at qopt and over-regularization beyond it. It does not describe the shape near p+q = n, so the double-descent shape cannot be read from the text.

source_check.notes: The supplied text is arXiv v4 dated 9 April 2020, although the record uses the initial preprint year 2018. Noise-driven and multiple-descent components of V6 are untested by the listed optimized-ridge comparison.

statements.correction: Spiked-covariance simulation: p = 1000, λopt = −150. MNIST random Fourier regression: n = 64, p = 2000; λopt ≈ −80 for the 80/100 training sets with s_min² > 100. The remaining 20/100 show diverging risk peaks at negative penalties. Over nonnegative penalties, MNIST risk is minimized at λ = 0.
statements.problem: The reported numbers are present, but the MNIST optimum near −80 applies only to a selected subset of training sets.
